title: Regionalism fades as the world shrinks
summary: In his youth people never travelled; now it is easy, and Europe's walls are down.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Until he came here. When he came here that was sort of permanent. Stravinsky left home when he was twenty seven, I think that's when he did the "Firebird". One can do it then; that's easy. One becomes a world citizen, which is the way the world is now anyway. I remember, we grew up in Nyack and there were kids I grew up with who had never been to New York City; things were that regional. It wasn't exactly an isolation but there was no real reason to do that. Peg came from up northern Wisconsin. Once in a while she'd go to Chicago and she didn't get out of there until she became a nurse and actually got
a job in the Veterans Administration in Illinois. I met her up there, but she began to move around.
But today, do you know anyone who hasn't been anywhere?
Not many. Not anyone who has never been anywhere.

I know still a lot of people though who maybe have ventured a little bit, but who basically stick pretty close to their own little province and rarely venture out. There's still a lot of that, I think.
You can still find a lot of people who live on Long Island or Westchester or Jersey who rarely come to New York City.
They might go to some shopping mall.
do they go to Europe, do they go to Maine, do they go off on vacation?
In many cases yes, I guess.

They didn't used to do that. If you went to Europe that's a big deal and when you did get to Europe, there was that evil wall around each country and it was a cultural, social national entity that goes back to medieval times. That's all flying apart today. Africa is a good example of it. That was one of the last places to go and certainly Asia. (Inaudible) That really changed, except for the British; that's something else. Now within fifty years it's all changed (inaudible). Maybe that's where we are. We have a chance to be that today and never before, so I think if we can use that chance

there is a possibility that we might get there instead of doing everything in terms of eighteenth, nineteenth century thinking, or even medieval thinking, but that goes slowly. People aren't prepared for it. Technology went too quick and w 're really not ready for that.
No, but I know about it.
You proably know everything he's got to say without having read it. You seem to know that instinct- ively.

A book like that is merely a collation of thoughts that have lead up to it. It's not an original thought. But if you work as a musician, you have to think about these things. It's very much a part of music.
